method: electroretinogram, light-adapted fish; sensitivity = -log10 of the threshold light intensity (threshold = visible deflection of the ERG trace) for each of nine test wavelengths (400, 440, 460, 480, 500, 520, 560, 600 and 670 nm) (20 ms flashes, 10 stimuli per wavelength, 5 s interval; photon flux at each wavelength measured with a USB 2000 spectrometer); 500 nm is the most sensitive of the nine tested wavelengths, not a fitted template peak; the paper groups 500 and 520 nm together as far more sensitive than 440, 600 and 670 nm
conditions: Wild-caught adult three-spined sticklebacks from the Oresund and southern Baltic coast of Skane, Sweden (experiment 4 fish caught 16 December 2012), air-freighted to Taiwan in July 2013, held in artificial brackish water (0.5% salinity) at 20 C on short day for 2 weeks, then 28 days of treatment; fish anaesthetised with MS-222, immobilised with gallamine triethiodide and light-adapted for 1 h on diffuse white background light (c. 12 lx); corneal recording electrode. Experiment 4 groups, 5 fish each: sham-operated males on long day (L16:D8), castrated males, castrated males with 11-ketoandrostenedione (11 KA) implants, and sham-operated males on short day (L8:D16); the 500 nm statement is not split by group. The same paper reports no significant difference in the 500 nm threshold between treatments (p > 0.05 for each comparison). The paper's main finding is that relative red sensitivity rose with androgen (600 and 670 nm, long day) and with long day (600 nm), with no significant difference at 670 nm between sham long and short day (p = 0.073); that is a separate result not logged here.
